newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - March 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - March 3.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories Monday:

* High-definition television equipment at station WHD-TV in Washington, D.C., calls for new sets and new backdrops to replace old ones made of cheaper materials and for more makeup on anchors who want to hide facial blemishes and wrinkles.

* Steven Brill, who founded the legal news empire that his former partner Time Warner is selling, ponders his future, including the possibilities of starting a journalism review and involvement in a multimedia enterprise.

* Classic Sports Network said it will file a complaint with the Federal Communications Commission against Cablevision Systems Corp accusing Cablevision of using coercive tactics to obtain an equity stake in Classic Sports.
* A Teamsters union has brought a shareholder resolution seeking to challenge the compensation of General Electric's chief executive, John Welch.
* CIENA, a small Internet technology company that recently went public, has achieved a $3.44 billion market valuation amid little publicity.
* MasterCard International said it is reviewing the advertising creative account it has had with Ammirati Puris Lintas since 1992.

* Sarah Frank, the chief executive of the British Broadcasting Corp's Americas unit, will resign after a restructuring from the BBC's joint venture pact with Discovery Communications, owned by Liberty Media Corp and three partners.

* Church of England officials may renew boycotts against infant formula makers such as Nestle AG in response to a report that the firms are violating international marketing codes meant to protect infant health in developing countries.
* Acclaim Entertainment hopes a new game, "Turok: Dinosaur Hunter," will reverse its declining stock price and profits.
* A Temple University radio station has canceled its contract with Pacifica Radio, which includes a commentary by a death row prisoner, raising accusations of censorship.

* New York State's unseasonably warm winter has left its municipal and county governments with some unexpected cash, but personal injury lawyers, ski resorts, sanitation workers and certain businesses are feeling the pinch.
